extraction.name: CommonsenseQA
extraction.description: A multiple-choice question answering dataset for commonsense reasoning, containing 12,247 questions generated by crowd workers based on concepts and relations from ConceptNet. Questions require prior world knowledge to answer, with five candidate answers per question.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.publisher: Tel-Aviv University / Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated by extracting subgraphs from ConceptNet, crowdsourcing question authoring and validation via Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), adding additional distractors, and collecting relevant web snippets via a search engine.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet knowledge base, specifically triplets filtered to 236,208 (q, r, a) triplets forming approximately 43,000 question sets, plus web snippets retrieved via search engine.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdsourcing workers authored three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), added two additional distractors per question, and verified questions' quality. A disjoint group of workers verified generated questions by annotating as unanswerable or choosing the right answer. Questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were kept, filtering out 15% of questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question is verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly are used. This process filters out 15% of the questions. Human accuracy on 100 sampled questions was 88.9% (majority vote from 5 workers).
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 workers for verification; 5 workers for human evaluation
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: CONCEPTNET knowledge base was used to extract subgraphs for question generation; Google Search was used to retrieve web snippets as textual context.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Commonsense datasets may contain distributional biases and annotation artifacts that allow models to achieve high performance without genuine understanding, by exploiting statistical patterns rather than reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Earlier commonsense datasets suffer from scalability issues (e.g., only 150 or 500-1000 examples), and annotation artifacts in datasets like Story Cloze Test allow models to perform well by ignoring the actual content, highlighting the difficulty of creating benchmarks that truly measure understanding.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating and benchmarking commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding, specifically as a question answering benchmark that tests common sense without requiring specialized scientific knowledge.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were generated from ConceptNet subgraphs, filtered by quality via crowdworkers, additional distractors were added, and textual context was added by querying a search engine for web snippets. Only annotators for which at least 75% of questions pass verification were accepted.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Triplets were filtered where one concept is more than four words or not in English, and where the edit distance between concepts is too low. Question sets were created by grouping three triplets sharing the same question concept and relation.

name.evidence: we present COMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering

description.evidence: We create 12,247 questions through this procedure and demonstrate the difficulty of our task with a large number of strong baselines... To capture common sense beyond associations, we extract from CONCEPTNET multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We generate multiple-choice questions in a process that comprises the following steps. 1. We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET... 2. We ask crowdsourcing workers to author three questions per subgraph... 3. We add textual context to each question by querying a search engine and retrieving web snippets.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers to generate and validate commonsense questions... We add textual context to each question by querying a search engine and retrieving web snippets.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: This results in a set of 236,208 triplets (q, r, a), where we call the first concept the question concept and the second concept the answer concept... The above procedure generates approximately 130,000 triplets (43,000 question sets), for which we can potentially generate questions.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We ask crowdsourcing workers to author three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), to add two additional distractors per question, and to verify questions' quality... We train a disjoint group of workers to verify the generated questions. Verifiers annotate a question as unanswerable, or choose the right answer.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: we did not use a qualification test, nor used AMT master workers

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Each question is verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly are used. This processes filters out 15% of the questions... Humans obtain 88.9% accuracy, taking a majority vote for each question.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: Each question is verified by 2 workers... we sampled 100 random questions and for each question gathered answers from five workers that were not involved in question generation.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts... We issue a web query to Google search for every question and candidate answer... We take the first 100 result snippets for each of the five answer candidates, yielding a context of 500 snippets per question.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Investigations of commonsense datasets, and of natural language datasets more generally, have revealed the difficulty in creating benchmarks that measure the understanding of a program rather than its ability to take advantage of distributional biases, and to model the annotation process.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: For both datasets, scalability is an issue when evaluating modern modeling approaches... Annotation artifacts in the Story Cloze Test, for example, allow models to achieve high performance while only looking at the proposed endings and ignoring the stories.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: In contrast to these efforts, our work studies common sense without requiring additional information... we create similarly well-crafted questions but at a larger scale.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: We add textual context to each question by querying a search engine and retrieving web snippets... we only accept annotators for which at least 75% of the questions they formulate pass the veriﬁcation process

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We ﬁlter triplets where one of the concepts is more than four words or not in English. We ﬁlter triplets where the edit distance between c1 and c2 is too low. This results in a set of 236,208 triplets
